Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Vignette:
Kwame is a sixty-three-year-old journalist who has spent decades covering conflict and human tragedy across the African continent, but the event that shattered him did not happen to him directly. It happened to his youngest daughter, Amara, during a visit to her university campus in Nairobi. She had called him to say she was caught in the middle of a student protest that had turned violent, and he could hear the chaos in the background—shouting, glass breaking, then a sound he still cannot name. He drove to the campus, pushed through crowds, and found her on the ground, bleeding from a wound to her head. In the hours that followed, as he sat with her in the emergency room, he remembers the taste of the coffee he had been drinking just before the call—bitter, metallic, somehow still present on his tongue even now, years later, whenever the memory returns. He recalls trying to explain to the triage nurse what had happened, but the words would not come. He knew the sequence of events perfectly—the call, the drive, the chaos, the blood—but when he opened his mouth, the sentences dissolved. He could not find the language to describe what he had seen, and the nurse had to ask him three times before he could point mutely at his daughter.

That inability to articulate the event has not faded. When friends or colleagues ask what happened, Kwame starts a sentence, then loses the thread. He knows the facts, but the words feel like they belong to someone else, or like they are buried under something heavy. He has stopped trying. At work, he has always been known for his precise, vivid reporting, but now he avoids writing about anything that involves loss. When his editor assigns him a piece about a family displaced by flooding, he requests a different topic. He cannot read the words “lost a loved one” without feeling his chest tighten. He has come to believe that if he lets himself think too long about what happened to Amara, he will fall apart entirely, and so he keeps his mind fixed on the present moment, on the next deadline, on the next story that does not touch on grief.

At home, his wife, Nkechi, has noticed that he no longer makes plans beyond the current week. When she mentions a vacation next summer or a retirement celebration for a friend, Kwame changes the subject or leaves the room. Talking about the future feels like a trap—a promise that something good might happen, which only reminds him how suddenly something terrible can come instead. He has come to believe that hope is dangerous, that looking forward is an invitation to disaster. Nkechi has tried to understand, but their conversations have grown strained. She wants to plan their daughter’s upcoming birthday dinner; he cannot bring himself to discuss it.

The worst moments come without warning. In a crowded café, he hears a cluster of incomprehensible chatter—three or four overlapping voices, none of them speaking clearly—and the sound plunges him back into the emergency room, where doctors and nurses spoke in rapid Swahili and English over Amara’s body. He cannot parse the noise now any more than he could then. The taste returns, metallic and sharp, and he has to leave the café without explanation. He has stopped going to public places where people gather in groups. He eats lunch at his desk, alone, with the door closed.

What finally brought him to seek help was a phone call from Amara herself, now fully recovered and living in another city. She told him she was pregnant, and he felt not joy but a wave of terror so complete that he could not respond. She asked if he was happy, and he said yes, but the word tasted like a lie. That night, he lay awake, unable to escape the image of her on the ground, and the taste of that coffee, and the certainty that he would not be able to protect her child any more than he had protected her. He came to the clinic because he is afraid of what will happen if he cannot find a way to speak about the future without feeling that he is tempting fate. He hopes, quietly, that someone can help him find the words he lost in that emergency room, but he is not sure they exist.
